```{r setup}
library(here); library(dplyr); library(knitr); library(survey)
source(here::here("R", "config.R"))
source(here::here("R", "02_prepare.R"))
source(here::here("R", "03_design.R"))
source(here::here("R", "utils_reliability.R"))
source(here::here("R", "04_descriptives.R"))
source(here::here("R", "05_models.R"))

cache <- here::here("data", "processed", "analytic.rds")
dat <- if (file.exists(cache)) readRDS(cache) else prepare_data(write_cache = TRUE)
design <- build_design(dat)
assert_full_design(design, nrow(dat))

descr  <- run_descriptives(design, write = FALSE)
models <- run_models(design, write = FALSE)

n_adults <- nrow(subset(design, is_adult == 1)$variables)
dfdesign <- survey::degf(subset(design, is_adult == 1))
ov <- descr$prevalence[descr$prevalence$group_variable == "Overall", ]
pct <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * x)
```

> **Independent portfolio project.** Not affiliated with CDC/NCHS. All findings are
> **associations** in cross-sectional data, never causal effects. Estimates are design-based
> (survey weights, strata, PSUs). Results describe **U.S.** adults and do **not** transfer to
> other health systems (e.g. Germany).

# Introduction

Regular dental-care use is unevenly distributed across the U.S. adult population. Using the
2017-2018 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES), this analysis describes
how **not having visited a dentist in the past 12 months** is associated with age, sex,
race/ethnicity, education, family income, self-rated oral health, and health-insurance
coverage. The analysis plan was pre-specified (`docs/analysis_plan.md`) and the measure
definitions were verified against the OHQ_J codebook (`docs/variable_map.md`) before any
association was estimated.

# Data & Methods

**Data.** NHANES 2017-2018 public-use files `DEMO_J` (demographics + survey design),
`OHQ_J` (oral-health questionnaire) and `HIQ_J` (insurance), merged on `SEQN`. Public-domain
CDC/NCHS data.

**Survey design.** The complex-survey design is built on the **full** `DEMO_J` sample
(`r format(nrow(dat), big.mark=",")` participants) with
`svydesign(id = ~SDMVPSU, strata = ~SDMVSTRA, weights = ~WTINT2YR, nest = TRUE)`. The
oral-health items are part of the in-home interview, so the **interview** weight `WTINT2YR`
is used (not the MEC weight). The analytic subpopulation --- interviewed adults aged 20+ ---
is taken as a survey **domain** via `subset()`, never by filtering before the design is built.
The design has **`r dfdesign` degrees of freedom**, used for all confidence intervals and tests.

**Outcome.** *No dental visit in the past 12 months*: `OHQ030 in {3,4,5,6,7}` vs `{1,2}`;
refused/don't-know recoded to missing. This is a **utilization indicator**, not proven unmet need.

**Estimation.** Weighted proportions with 95% Korn-Graubard ("beta") confidence intervals
(`svyciprop`), with the unweighted denominator shown alongside. Estimate reliability follows
the NCHS Data Presentation Standards for Proportions (Parker et al. 2017). Associations are
modelled with `svyglm`: **odds ratios** (`quasibinomial`) and **prevalence ratios**
(`quasipoisson`, log link), because the outcome is common and odds ratios then overstate the
relative risk. Wald tests (`regTermTest`) assess categorical terms. Full code is in `R/`.

# Results

Of `r format(nrow(dat), big.mark=",")` NHANES participants, **`r format(n_adults, big.mark=",")`**
were interviewed adults aged 20+. Overall, **`r pct(ov$estimate)`** (95% CI
`r pct(ov$ci_low)`-`r pct(ov$ci_high)`) had **no dental visit in the past 12 months**.

## Sample characteristics (Table 1)

```{r table1}
descr$table1 |>
  dplyr::transmute(Variable = variable, Level = level,
                   `n (unweighted)` = n_unweighted,
                   `Weighted %` = sprintf("%.1f", weighted_pct)) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

## No recent dental visit, by group

Weighted prevalence with 95% CIs; open markers denote NCHS reliability-flagged estimates.

```{r prev-fig, fig.height=9}
make_prevalence_figure(descr$prevalence)
```

```{r prev-tab}
descr$prevalence |>
  dplyr::filter(group_variable != "Overall") |>
  dplyr::transmute(Group = group_variable, Level = group_level,
                   `Prevalence` = pct(estimate),
                   `95% CI` = paste0(pct(ci_low), "-", pct(ci_high)),
                   `n` = n_unweighted, Reliability = reliability_flag) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

## Reason for last visit and self-reported unmet need

Among adults with a visit in the past 12 months, the main reason was predominantly
preventive (`r sprintf("%.0f%%", descr$reason$weighted_pct[descr$reason$reason=="Preventive"])`
preventive vs `r sprintf("%.0f%%", descr$reason$weighted_pct[descr$reason$reason=="Problem-driven"])`
problem-driven). Separately, **`r pct(descr$unmet$estimate[descr$unmet$group_variable=="Overall"])`**
of adults reported needing dental care in the past year but being unable to get it; the most
common reason was cost.

```{r unmet-reasons}
descr$unmet_reasons |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(weighted_pct)) |>
  dplyr::transmute(`Reason unmet need could not be met` = reason_label,
                   `Weighted %` = sprintf("%.1f", weighted_pct),
                   `n endorsed` = n_endorsed) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

## Adjusted associations

Adjusted odds ratios (model b: all sociodemographic covariates) for no recent dental visit:

```{r forest, fig.height=7}
make_forest(models$coefficients)
```

```{r coef-tab}
models$coefficients |>
  dplyr::filter(model == "Adjusted (b)") |>
  dplyr::transmute(Measure = measure, Term = term,
                   Estimate = sprintf("%.2f", estimate),
                   `95% CI` = sprintf("%.2f-%.2f", ci_low, ci_high),
                   p = signif(p_value, 2)) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

Overall tests of each categorical term (Wald, design df):

```{r wald-tab}
models$wald |>
  dplyr::filter(model == "Adjusted (b)") |>
  dplyr::transmute(Term = term, `num df` = df, `den df` = ddf,
                   F = sprintf("%.1f", F), p = signif(p_value, 2)) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

Odds ratios are larger than the corresponding prevalence ratios (e.g. lowest income band),
as expected for a common outcome; the prevalence ratios are the more conservative measure of
relative difference.

## Sensitivity analysis: missing income

`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100*mean(is.na(dat$INDFMPIR[dat$is_adult==1])))` of adults were missing
family income. The primary model uses complete cases; a missing-indicator model retaining the
full sample gives materially similar income associations:

```{r sens-tab}
models$sensitivity |>
  dplyr::filter(grepl("income", term)) |>
  dplyr::transmute(Model = model, Term = term,
                   OR = sprintf("%.2f", estimate),
                   `95% CI` = sprintf("%.2f-%.2f", ci_low, ci_high), n = n) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

# Discussion

Lower education, lower family income, being uninsured, and worse self-rated oral health are
each **associated with** a higher prevalence of not having a recent dental visit, and the
income and education gradients persist after mutual adjustment. Younger adults and men were
also more likely to report no recent visit. These patterns are consistent with well-documented
socioeconomic inequalities in dental-care access in the United States, where dental coverage is
often separate from medical insurance and routine dental care is excluded from traditional
Medicare. Because the outcome is common, prevalence ratios (reported alongside odds ratios) give
a more interpretable sense of the relative differences.

# Limitations

- **Cross-sectional**: associations only; no causal or temporal inference.
- **Self-report**: dental-visit timing and oral-health rating are subject to recall and
  social-desirability bias.
- "No recent visit" is a **utilization indicator**, not equivalent to unmet need.
- Data are **2017-2018**, before the COVID-19 pandemic.
- **U.S. sample**: results do **not** transfer to other systems (e.g. Germany), which differ in
  insurance and dental-care organization.
- ~13% of adults were missing family income; sensitivity analysis addresses but does not
  eliminate this.
- Small subgroups carry wide CIs; NCHS-flagged estimates are marked.
